blocks.text: Alternating current and voltage

A battery drives a **direct current** (DC): its value and direction stay the same. The electricity supplied to homes and factories is different. Its voltage rises from zero to a maximum, falls back through zero, reverses, reaches a maximum in the opposite direction and returns to zero, over and over again. Such a voltage is an **alternating voltage**, and the current it drives is an **alternating current** (AC).

AC is preferred for power distribution for two main reasons. First, generators based on a rotating coil produce it naturally. Second, and more important, an alternating voltage can be stepped up or down efficiently with a transformer, so electrical power can be sent over long distances at high voltage and low current, with small losses, and then reduced to a safe voltage for use. A transformer cannot do this with DC.

A current whose magnitude changes continuously with time and whose direction reverses periodically. In the simplest and most important case it varies sinusoidally, $i = I_0\sin\omega t$. An alternating voltage is defined in the same way, $v = V_0\sin\omega t$. SI units: ampere (A) and volt (V).

blocks.latex: v = V_0\sin\omega t \qquad i = I_0\sin\omega t \qquad \omega = 2\pi\nu = \frac{2\pi}{T}
blocks.text: $V_0, I_0$ = peak values (amplitudes) in V and A; $\omega$ = angular frequency ($\text{rad s}^{-1}$); $\nu$ = frequency, the number of complete cycles per second (Hz); $T$ = time period, the time for one complete cycle (s).

The graph shows one cycle and a little more of a sinusoidal current. During the first half of the cycle (from 0 to $T/2$) the current is positive; it reaches its peak $+I_0$ at $t = T/4$. During the second half it is negative and reaches $-I_0$ at $t = 3T/4$. At $t = T$ the cycle starts again. Because the current passes through zero twice in every cycle, its direction reverses $2\nu$ times per second.

For the Indian mains, $\nu = 50\,\text{Hz}$, so $\omega = 2\pi \times 50 = 100\pi \approx 314\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$ and $T = 0.02\,\text{s} = 20\,\text{ms}$. The current changes direction 100 times every second.

Indian domestic supply: 220 V (rms), 50 Hz. Its peak value is $220\sqrt{2} \approx 311\,\text{V}$, and its direction reverses 100 times per second. A frequency of 50 Hz means 50 complete cycles, not 50 reversals, per second.
Peak, average and rms values
The maximum value, $I_0$ or $V_0$, that an alternating current or voltage reaches in either direction during a cycle. The peak-to-peak value is $2I_0$.

**Average value.** Over one complete cycle a sinusoidal current is positive for half the time and equally negative for the other half, so its average over a full cycle is **zero**. That does not mean it does nothing: a heater works just as well on AC as on DC, because the heating effect depends on $i^2$, which is never negative. For rectifier circuits one sometimes needs the average over a **half** cycle:

$$\bar{i}_{\text{half}} = \frac{1}{T/2}\int_0^{T/2} I_0\sin\omega t\,dt = \frac{2I_0}{\pi} \approx 0.637\,I_0$$

**Root-mean-square value.** To compare AC with DC we compare their heating effects. In a resistor $R$ the heat produced in one period is

$$H = \int_0^T i^2R\,dt = I_0^2R\int_0^T \sin^2\omega t\,dt$$

Using $\sin^2\omega t = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 - \cos 2\omega t)$ and the fact that $\cos 2\omega t$ averages to zero over a period, the integral equals $T/2$. So $H = \tfrac{1}{2}I_0^2RT$. A steady current $I$ would produce $I^2RT$ in the same time. Equating the two gives $I^2 = I_0^2/2$, i.e. $I = I_0/\sqrt{2}$. This $I$ is the square root of the mean of $i^2$, hence the name root-mean-square (rms) value.

The rms value of an alternating current is the value of the steady direct current that would produce the same amount of heat in a given resistor in the same time. It equals the square root of the mean of $i^2$ over one cycle. For a sinusoidal current, $I_{\text{rms}} = I_0/\sqrt{2}$. SI unit: ampere (for voltage, volt).
Valid for sinusoidal AC. $I_0, V_0$ = peak values. In this lesson $I$ and $V$ without a subscript mean rms values.

AC ammeters and voltmeters are calibrated to read rms values, and the ratings printed on appliances (220 V, 5 A) are rms values. Whenever an AC voltage or current is quoted without saying otherwise, it is the rms value. Insulation and capacitors, however, must be able to withstand the **peak** voltage, which is about 1.41 times the rms value.

blocks.text:
**Common mistakes.**
- Quoted mains voltages (220 V) are rms, not peak; the peak is 311 V.
- Power formulas use rms values: $P = V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi$, which equals $\tfrac{1}{2}V_0I_0\cos\phi$. Do not multiply peak values without the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
- The relation $I_{\text{rms}} = I_0/\sqrt{2}$ holds only for sinusoidal waveforms. For a square wave of height $I_0$, the rms value equals $I_0$.

blocks.problem: The domestic supply is 220 V, 50 Hz. (a) Find the peak voltage and write the equation of the voltage. (b) A bulb rated 100 W, 220 V is connected to this supply. Find its resistance, the rms current and the peak current. (c) How long does the voltage take to rise from zero to its peak value?
blocks.solution:
(a) The quoted 220 V is the rms value, so the peak voltage is $V_0 = \sqrt{2}\,V = 1.414 \times 220 = 311\,\text{V}$. The angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi\nu = 100\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$, so the voltage can be written as $v = 311\sin(100\pi t)\,\text{V}$.

(b) The rated power and voltage are rms values, so $R = V^2/P = (220)^2/100 = 484\,\Omega$. The rms current is $I = P/V = 100/220 = 0.455\,\text{A}$, and the peak current is $I_0 = \sqrt{2}\,I = 0.643\,\text{A}$.

(c) The voltage goes from zero to its peak in a quarter of a period. The period is $T = 1/50 = 0.02\,\text{s}$, so the time is $T/4 = 0.005\,\text{s} = 5\,\text{ms}$.

blocks.text: Phasors and phasor diagrams

In AC circuits we constantly have to add voltages that have the same frequency but different phases. Adding expressions such as $a\sin\omega t + b\sin(\omega t + \pi/2)$ by trigonometry is slow. A **phasor diagram** turns this into simple geometry.

A rotating vector that represents a sinusoidally varying quantity. Its length equals the peak value of the quantity, it rotates anticlockwise about the origin with angular speed $\omega$, and its projection on the vertical axis at any instant gives the instantaneous value of the quantity. A phasor making angle $\omega t + \phi_0$ with the horizontal axis represents $V_0\sin(\omega t + \phi_0)$.

Key rules for using phasors:

- All phasors of a circuit rotate together at the same $\omega$, so the **angles between them stay fixed**. The angle between two phasors is the phase difference between the two quantities.
- A phasor that is ahead in the anticlockwise sense **leads**; the other **lags**.
- The sum of two sinusoidal quantities of the same frequency is represented by the vector sum of their phasors (parallelogram or triangle rule).
- Since only the relative angles matter, we usually draw a phasor diagram at one convenient instant, for example with the current phasor along the horizontal axis.
- Phasors are not vectors in physical space; they are a geometric bookkeeping tool for phases.

The figure shows the phasor relations for the three basic circuit elements. Each is derived in the next three sections.
AC voltage applied to a resistor

Connect a resistor $R$ to a source $v = V_0\sin\omega t$. By Kirchhoff's loop rule $v = iR$ at every instant, so

$$i = \frac{V_0}{R}\sin\omega t = I_0\sin\omega t, \qquad I_0 = \frac{V_0}{R}$$

The current and the voltage reach their maxima, zeros and minima at the same instants: they are **in phase**, and their phasors point in the same direction (panel a). Ohm's law holds for peak values and for rms values, $V = IR$, and the resistance does not depend on frequency.

The instantaneous power $p = i^2R = I_0^2R\sin^2\omega t$ is always positive. Its average over a cycle is $\bar{p} = \tfrac{1}{2}I_0^2R = I^2R = V^2/R$. A resistor always takes energy from the source and converts it into heat.
AC voltage applied to an inductor: inductive reactance

Connect a pure inductor $L$ (zero resistance) to $v = V_0\sin\omega t$. The changing current produces a back emf $-L\,di/dt$, and Kirchhoff's loop rule gives $v - L\,\dfrac{di}{dt} = 0$, i.e.

$$\frac{di}{dt} = \frac{V_0}{L}\sin\omega t$$

Integrating (the constant must be zero, because the current oscillates about zero):

$$i = -\frac{V_0}{\omega L}\cos\omega t = \frac{V_0}{\omega L}\sin\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$

So the current amplitude is $I_0 = V_0/(\omega L)$, and the current **lags the voltage by $\pi/2$** (a quarter of a period, $T/4$). The quantity $\omega L$ plays the role of resistance and is called the inductive reactance.

The opposition offered by an inductor to alternating current, $X_L = \omega L = 2\pi\nu L$. It is the ratio of the peak (or rms) voltage across a pure inductor to the peak (or rms) current through it. SI unit: ohm ($\Omega$).
$L$ = inductance (H); $\nu$ = frequency (Hz); $X_L$ in ohm. $X_L$ is directly proportional to frequency: it is zero for DC and very large at high frequencies.

**Physical picture.** The faster the current changes, the larger the back emf, so an inductor opposes high-frequency currents strongly and lets steady current through freely. The voltage peaks when the current is changing fastest, which is when the current is passing through zero; the current peaks a quarter cycle later. The graph (panel a) shows this lag.

**Power.** The instantaneous power is $p = vi = V_0I_0\sin\omega t\,\sin(\omega t - \pi/2) = -\tfrac{1}{2}V_0I_0\sin 2\omega t$, which is positive for one quarter cycle and negative for the next. Its average over a cycle is **zero**. During one quarter cycle the inductor stores energy $\tfrac{1}{2}LI_0^2$ in its magnetic field; during the next it returns that energy to the source. An ideal inductor consumes no power.
AC voltage applied to a capacitor: capacitive reactance

Connect a capacitor $C$ to $v = V_0\sin\omega t$. At each instant the charge on it is $q = Cv = CV_0\sin\omega t$. The current is the rate of flow of charge:

$$i = \frac{dq}{dt} = \omega CV_0\cos\omega t = \frac{V_0}{1/(\omega C)}\sin\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$

The current amplitude is $I_0 = V_0/(1/\omega C)$, and the current **leads the voltage by $\pi/2$**. The current is largest when the voltage is zero but changing fastest, and it is zero when the voltage is at its peak and momentarily not changing. Charge does not actually cross the gap between the plates; the capacitor is repeatedly charged and discharged, so current flows in the connecting wires.

The opposition offered by a capacitor to alternating current, $X_C = 1/(\omega C) = 1/(2\pi\nu C)$. It is the ratio of the peak (or rms) voltage across the capacitor to the peak (or rms) current. SI unit: ohm ($\Omega$).
$C$ = capacitance (F); $\nu$ = frequency (Hz); $X_C$ in ohm. $X_C$ is inversely proportional to frequency: infinite for DC (a capacitor blocks steady current) and very small at high frequencies.

**Power.** Here $p = vi = V_0I_0\sin\omega t\cos\omega t = \tfrac{1}{2}V_0I_0\sin 2\omega t$, whose average over a cycle is again **zero**. The capacitor stores energy $\tfrac{1}{2}CV_0^2$ in its electric field during one quarter cycle and gives it back during the next. An ideal capacitor, like an ideal inductor, consumes no average power.

A memory aid for the phase relations is the word **CIVIL**: in a **C**apacitor, **I** leads **V**; **V** leads **I** in an inductor **L**.

blocks.problem: (a) A pure inductor of 0.20 H is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find its reactance, the rms current and the peak current. What happens to the current if the frequency is doubled? (b) A $50\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor is connected to the same supply. Find its reactance and the rms current.
blocks.solution:
(a) The inductive reactance is $X_L = 2\pi\nu L = 2\pi \times 50 \times 0.20 = 62.8\,\Omega$. The rms current is $I = V/X_L = 220/62.8 = 3.50\,\text{A}$, and the peak current is $I_0 = \sqrt{2}\,I = 4.95\,\text{A}$. If the frequency is doubled, $X_L$ doubles to $125.7\,\Omega$, so the current is halved to about 1.75 A.

(b) The capacitive reactance is $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\nu C} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 50\times10^{-6}} = 63.7\,\Omega$. The rms current is $I = V/X_C = 220/63.7 = 3.46\,\text{A}$. Doubling the frequency would halve $X_C$ and double this current, the opposite of the inductor's behaviour.
blocks.answer: (a) 62.8 Ω, 3.50 A, 4.95 A; current halves to about 1.75 A (b) 63.7 Ω, 3.46 A

blocks.text: Reactance and impedance

Resistance and reactance are both measured in ohms and both limit the current, but they are physically different.

- **Resistance** converts electrical energy into heat. It does not depend on frequency, and the voltage across a resistor is in phase with the current.
- **Reactance** ($X_L$ or $X_C$) only stores energy and returns it, so it causes no average power loss. It depends on frequency, and the voltage across it is $90^\circ$ out of phase with the current.

In a circuit that contains both, the total opposition to the current is called the **impedance**. Because resistive and reactive voltages are $90^\circ$ apart, they combine like the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle, not by simple addition. In the **impedance triangle**, $R$ is the base, the net reactance $X = X_L - X_C$ is the height, the impedance $Z$ is the hypotenuse, and the angle between $Z$ and $R$ is the phase angle $\phi$. The inductive and capacitive reactances subtract because the voltages across $L$ and $C$ are exactly opposite in phase.

The total effective opposition of an AC circuit to the current, equal to the ratio of the peak voltage to the peak current (or of the rms voltage to the rms current): $Z = V_0/I_0 = V/I$. For a series LCR circuit $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$. SI unit: ohm ($\Omega$).

blocks.text: Series LCR circuit

Now connect a resistor $R$, an inductor $L$ and a capacitor $C$ in series with a source $v = V_0\sin\omega t$. Because they are in series, the **same current** flows through all three at every instant, so the current is the natural reference phasor. Let its amplitude be $I_0$.

- The voltage across $R$ has amplitude $V_{R0} = I_0R$ and is **in phase** with the current.
- The voltage across $L$ has amplitude $V_{L0} = I_0X_L$ and **leads** the current by $90^\circ$.
- The voltage across $C$ has amplitude $V_{C0} = I_0X_C$ and **lags** the current by $90^\circ$.

The phasors of $V_L$ and $V_C$ therefore point in exactly opposite directions, and their resultant is $V_{L0} - V_{C0}$ (taking $X_L > X_C$ for the figure). This resultant is perpendicular to $V_{R0}$, so the source voltage, which is the phasor sum of all three, is the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

**Impedance.** From the right triangle in the phasor diagram,

$$V_0^2 = V_{R0}^2 + (V_{L0} - V_{C0})^2 = I_0^2\left[R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2\right]$$

so $I_0 = V_0/Z$ with $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.

**Phase angle.** The source voltage leads the current by the angle $\phi$ given by $\tan\phi = (V_{L0} - V_{C0})/V_{R0} = (X_L - X_C)/R$. Equivalently, if the source voltage is written as $v = V_0\sin\omega t$, the current is $i = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$.

- If $X_L > X_C$, $\phi$ is positive: the circuit is **inductive** and the current lags the voltage.
- If $X_L < X_C$, $\phi$ is negative: the circuit is **capacitive** and the current leads the voltage.
- If $X_L = X_C$, $\phi = 0$: the current is in phase with the voltage. This is **resonance**, discussed next.
$Z$ = impedance ($\Omega$); $R$ = resistance; $X_L = \omega L$ and $X_C = 1/(\omega C)$ = reactances; $V_0, I_0$ = peak values and $V, I$ = rms values of the source voltage and the current.

$\phi$ = phase angle by which the source voltage leads the current. Some books define the angle by which the current leads the voltage, $\tan\phi' = (X_C - X_L)/R$; it is the same physics with the opposite sign.

**Common mistakes in LCR problems.**
- The source voltage is **not** $V_R + V_L + V_C$. Add them as phasors: $V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$.
- The rms voltage across $L$ or across $C$ can be larger than the source voltage. This is not a mistake: the two partly cancel each other.
- Reactances subtract, $X_L - X_C$, because $V_L$ and $V_C$ are $180^\circ$ out of phase. Never add them.
- For an RL circuit put $X_C = 0$; for an RC circuit put $X_L = 0$ in the same formulas.

blocks.problem: A series LCR circuit has $R = 80\,\Omega$, $L = 0.20\,\text{H}$ and $C = 50\,\mu\text{F}$. It is connected to a 200 V (rms) source of angular frequency $500\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$. Find (a) the reactances and the impedance, (b) the rms current, (c) the rms voltages across R, L and C, and check that they combine to give the source voltage, (d) the phase angle and whether the current leads or lags.
blocks.solution:
(a) The inductive reactance is $X_L = \omega L = 500 \times 0.20 = 100\,\Omega$. The capacitive reactance is $X_C = 1/(\omega C) = 1/(500 \times 50\times10^{-6}) = 40\,\Omega$. The impedance is $Z = \sqrt{80^2 + (100 - 40)^2} = \sqrt{6400 + 3600} = 100\,\Omega$.

(b) The rms current is $I = V/Z = 200/100 = 2.0\,\text{A}$.

(c) The voltages are $V_R = IR = 160\,\text{V}$, $V_L = IX_L = 200\,\text{V}$ and $V_C = IX_C = 80\,\text{V}$. Their phasor sum is $\sqrt{160^2 + (200 - 80)^2} = \sqrt{25600 + 14400} = 200\,\text{V}$, equal to the source voltage. Their simple sum, 440 V, is meaningless. Note that $V_L$ alone equals the source voltage.

(d) $\tan\phi = (X_L - X_C)/R = 60/80 = 0.75$, so $\phi = 36.9^\circ$. Since $X_L > X_C$, the circuit is inductive and the current lags the source voltage by $36.9^\circ$.

blocks.text: Resonance in a series LCR circuit

Keep $R$, $L$, $C$ and the source voltage fixed and slowly increase the frequency. The inductive reactance $X_L = \omega L$ rises steadily, while the capacitive reactance $X_C = 1/(\omega C)$ falls. At one particular angular frequency $\omega_0$ they become equal. There the net reactance vanishes, the impedance has its smallest possible value $Z = R$, and the current amplitude is largest, $I_{\text{max}} = V/R$. The current is in phase with the source voltage, and the circuit behaves as if it contained only the resistor. Setting $\omega_0 L = 1/(\omega_0 C)$ gives the resonant frequency.

The condition in which the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal, $X_L = X_C$, so that the impedance is minimum ($Z = R$), the current is maximum and in phase with the applied voltage. It occurs at the resonant frequency $\nu_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$, measured in hertz (Hz).
$\omega_0$ = resonant angular frequency ($\text{rad s}^{-1}$); $\nu_0$ = resonant frequency (Hz); $L$ in henry, $C$ in farad. The resonant frequency does not depend on $R$.

**Resonance curve.** The figure plots the rms current against $\omega$ for two circuits with the same $L$ and $C$ but different resistances. Both peak at the same $\omega_0$, since $\omega_0$ does not involve $R$. The circuit with the smaller resistance has a taller and narrower peak: it responds strongly only to frequencies very close to $\omega_0$. Far from resonance the reactances dominate and both curves nearly coincide.

**Sharpness and quality factor.** The frequencies $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ at which the current falls to $I_{\text{max}}/\sqrt{2}$ are the half-power points, because the power $I^2R$ there is half its maximum. The interval between them is the **bandwidth**, $2\Delta\omega = \omega_2 - \omega_1 = R/L$. The sharpness of resonance is measured by the **quality factor**, $Q = \omega_0/(2\Delta\omega) = \omega_0L/R$. A small $R$ means a small bandwidth, a large $Q$ and a sharp resonance.

**Voltage magnification.** At resonance the voltage across the inductor is $V_L = I\omega_0L = (V/R)\omega_0L = QV$, and the voltage across the capacitor is equal and opposite. With a large $Q$ these voltages can be many times the source voltage even though they cancel each other in the total.

**Resonance needs both L and C.** In an RL or an RC circuit there is only one kind of reactance, nothing can cancel it, and there is no resonance.

**Application: tuning.** The aerial of a radio receives signals from many stations at once. Turning the tuning knob changes $C$ (or $L$) until the resonant frequency equals the frequency of the desired station. The circuit then responds strongly to that station and weakly to all others; a high $Q$ gives good selectivity.
$Q$ = quality factor (a pure number); $2\Delta\omega$ = bandwidth between the half-power frequencies ($\text{rad s}^{-1}$). At resonance $V_L = V_C = QV$, where $V$ is the source voltage.

blocks.problem: A series LCR circuit with $L = 25\,\text{mH}$, $C = 0.40\,\mu\text{F}$ and $R = 10\,\Omega$ is connected to a variable-frequency source of rms voltage 5.0 V. Find (a) the resonant angular frequency and frequency, (b) the rms current at resonance, (c) the rms voltage across the inductor at resonance, (d) the quality factor and the bandwidth.
blocks.solution:
(a) First find $LC = 0.025 \times 0.40\times10^{-6} = 1.0\times10^{-8}\,\text{s}^2$, so $\sqrt{LC} = 1.0\times10^{-4}\,\text{s}$. The resonant angular frequency is $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC} = 1.0\times10^{4}\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$, and the frequency is $\nu_0 = \omega_0/2\pi = 1.59\times10^{3}\,\text{Hz}$, about 1.6 kHz.

(b) At resonance the impedance equals the resistance, so $I = V/R = 5.0/10 = 0.50\,\text{A}$.

(c) The inductive reactance at resonance is $X_L = \omega_0L = 10^4 \times 0.025 = 250\,\Omega$, so $V_L = IX_L = 0.50 \times 250 = 125\,\text{V}$. This is 25 times the source voltage; the capacitor has an equal and opposite 125 V across it.

(d) The quality factor is $Q = \omega_0L/R = 250/10 = 25$, which matches $V_L/V = 125/5$. The bandwidth is $2\Delta\omega = R/L = 10/0.025 = 400\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$.
blocks.answer: (a) 1.0 × 10⁴ rad/s, about 1.59 kHz (b) 0.50 A (c) 125 V (d) Q = 25, bandwidth 400 rad/s

blocks.text: Power in an AC circuit

Let the source voltage be $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ and the current $i = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$. The instantaneous power delivered by the source is

$$p = vi = V_0I_0\sin\omega t\,\sin(\omega t - \phi) = \frac{V_0I_0}{2}\left[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t - \phi)\right]$$

using $2\sin A\sin B = \cos(A - B) - \cos(A + B)$. The second term oscillates at frequency $2\omega$ and averages to zero over a cycle. The average power is therefore

$$P = \frac{V_0I_0}{2}\cos\phi = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\phi = VI\cos\phi$$

where $V$ and $I$ are rms values. The product $VI$ is called the **apparent power** (measured in volt-ampere, VA); the actual average power $VI\cos\phi$ is the **true** or **active power** (watt, W).

Since $\cos\phi = R/Z$ and $V = IZ$, the true power can also be written $P = I^2Z \cdot (R/Z) = I^2R$. Only the resistance consumes energy on average; the inductor and capacitor merely exchange energy back and forth with the source.

$P$ = average (true) power (W); $V_{\text{rms}}, I_{\text{rms}}$ = rms voltage and current; $V_0, I_0$ = peak values; $\phi$ = phase difference between voltage and current; $R$ = total resistance of the circuit ($\Omega$).
Power factor
The factor $\cos\phi$ in $P = VI\cos\phi$; the ratio of the true power to the apparent power, $\cos\phi = P/(VI) = R/Z$. It is a pure number between 0 and 1 and has no unit.

blocks.caption: Power factor and average power in different circuits

blocks.text:
**Why power factor matters.** For a given power $P$ at a given voltage $V$, the current drawn is $I = P/(V\cos\phi)$. A low power factor means a large current for the same useful power. The extra current produces extra $I^2R$ losses in the supply cables and transformers and needs thicker wires. Factories with many motors (which are inductive) often have power factors well below 1, and supply companies charge them for it.

The remedy is **power-factor correction**: capacitors are connected across the inductive load. The capacitor draws a current that leads the voltage, cancelling much of the lagging reactive current of the motors. The phase angle $\phi$ is reduced, $\cos\phi$ moves towards 1, and the line current falls while the useful power is unchanged.

blocks.problem: A device with resistance $30\,\Omega$ and inductive reactance $40\,\Omega$ in series is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find (a) the impedance and rms current, (b) the power factor, (c) the average power consumed, and check it with $I^2R$, (d) the active and wattless components of the current.
blocks.solution:
(a) The impedance is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50\,\Omega$, so the rms current is $I = V/Z = 220/50 = 4.4\,\text{A}$.

(b) The power factor is $\cos\phi = R/Z = 30/50 = 0.6$; the current lags the voltage because the circuit is inductive. Correspondingly $\sin\phi = X_L/Z = 0.8$.

(c) The average power is $P = VI\cos\phi = 220 \times 4.4 \times 0.6 = 580.8\,\text{W}$. Checking with the resistor alone, $I^2R = (4.4)^2 \times 30 = 19.36 \times 30 = 580.8\,\text{W}$, the same, as it must be.

(d) The active component, in phase with the voltage, is $I\cos\phi = 4.4 \times 0.6 = 2.64\,\text{A}$. The wattless component, at right angles to the voltage, is $I\sin\phi = 4.4 \times 0.8 = 3.52\,\text{A}$. Note that $\sqrt{2.64^2 + 3.52^2} = 4.4\,\text{A}$.
blocks.answer: (a) 50 Ω, 4.4 A (b) 0.6 (lagging) (c) 580.8 W (d) 2.64 A active, 3.52 A wattless

blocks.text: Wattless current

The current phasor $I$ makes an angle $\phi$ with the voltage phasor $V$. Resolve it into two perpendicular components, as in the figure:

- $I\cos\phi$, along $V$ (in phase with the voltage). Only this component carries average power: $P = V(I\cos\phi)$. It is called the **active** or **wattful** component.
- $I\sin\phi$, perpendicular to $V$ ($90^\circ$ out of phase with the voltage). Like the current in a pure inductor or capacitor, it gives zero average power. It is called the **wattless** or **idle** current.

The component of an alternating current, $I\sin\phi$, that is $90^\circ$ out of phase with the voltage and therefore consumes no average power. In a purely inductive or purely capacitive circuit ($\phi = 90^\circ$) the entire current is wattless. SI unit: ampere.

blocks.latex: I_{\text{active}} = I\cos\phi \qquad I_{\text{wattless}} = I\sin\phi \qquad I = \sqrt{I_{\text{active}}^2 + I_{\text{wattless}}^2}
blocks.text: $I$ = rms current (A); $\phi$ = phase angle between voltage and current. Average power $P = V I_{\text{active}}$.

**Application: the choke coil.** Suppose a lamp needs a smaller current than the mains would drive through it. A series resistor could reduce the current, but it would waste power as heat, $I^2R$. A **choke coil**, an inductor with very small resistance, reduces the current just as well through its reactance, yet the current through it is almost wattless, so very little power is lost. Chokes were used for this reason in fluorescent tube lights. The wattless current still flows in the wires, though, and still causes some heating in them, which is why a low power factor is undesirable on a large scale.

blocks.problem: A lamp rated 100 V, 1.0 A is to be run from a 200 V, 50 Hz supply. (a) What resistance must be connected in series with it, and how much power is wasted in that resistor? (b) What pure inductance (choke) in series would do the same job, and how much power would it waste?
blocks.solution:
The lamp behaves as a resistance $R = 100/1.0 = 100\,\Omega$ and must carry a current of 1.0 A.

(a) With a series resistor the total resistance must be $200/1.0 = 200\,\Omega$, so the extra resistance is $100\,\Omega$. The power wasted in it is $I^2R = 1.0^2 \times 100 = 100\,\text{W}$, as much as the lamp itself uses.

(b) With a choke the impedance must be $Z = 200/1.0 = 200\,\Omega$. So $\sqrt{100^2 + X_L^2} = 200$, which gives $X_L = \sqrt{40000 - 10000} = 173\,\Omega$. The inductance is $L = X_L/(2\pi\nu) = 173/(2\pi \times 50) = 0.55\,\text{H}$. A pure inductor consumes no average power, because its current is wattless with respect to its own voltage, so the power wasted is zero; a real choke wastes only a little in its small resistance.
blocks.answer: (a) 100 Ω, wasting 100 W (b) about 0.55 H, wasting (ideally) no power

blocks.text: **Wattless does not mean currentless.** A wattless current is a real current that you can measure with an ammeter; it simply delivers no net energy, because the energy it carries in one quarter cycle is returned in the next. Questions often ask for $I\sin\phi$ given $V$, $I$ and $P$: first find $\cos\phi = P/(VI)$, then $\sin\phi = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2\phi}$.
Revision summary

blocks.caption: Formula sheet: alternating currents
rows: 1 at resonance, 0 for pure L or C

blocks.text:
- Meters and ratings give rms values; peak $= \sqrt{2} \times$ rms for sinusoidal AC.
- $X_L$ grows with frequency and $X_C$ falls with it; an inductor passes DC and a capacitor blocks it.
- In series LCR the same current flows everywhere; voltages add as phasors, never arithmetically.
- At resonance $X_L = X_C$, $Z = R$, the current is maximum, $\cos\phi = 1$, and $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$ is independent of $R$.
- Average power is $VI\cos\phi$; pure inductors and capacitors consume none, and their current is wattless.

In a series LCR circuit at resonance the voltage across $L$ (or $C$) is $Q$ times the source voltage. With $Q = 25$ and a 5 V source, 125 V appears across the inductor, which is why components in tuned circuits must be rated for voltages far above the supply voltage.

**Exam tips.**
- Check whether a question gives peak or rms values; equations like $v = 311\sin 100\pi t$ give the peak, so divide by $\sqrt{2}$ for rms.
- From $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ and $i = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$ read off $\phi$ directly and use $P = \tfrac{1}{2}V_0I_0\cos\phi$.
- A 'circuit behaves as purely resistive' statement means resonance: use $X_L = X_C$.
- If only $V$, $I$ and $P$ are given, $\cos\phi = P/VI$.
- Microfarads and millihenries: convert to farads and henries before using the formulas.

questions.stem: An alternating current is given by $i = 5\sin(100\pi t)$ A, where $t$ is in seconds. The frequency of this current is
questions.explanation: Compare the given expression with the standard form $i = I_0\sin\omega t$. The coefficient of time is the angular frequency, $\omega = 100\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$. Because the angular frequency equals $2\pi$ times the frequency, the frequency is $\nu = 100\pi/2\pi = 50\,\text{Hz}$. The peak current of 5 A plays no part in deciding the frequency.

optionRationale.1: This divides $100\pi$ by $\pi$ only; dividing by $2\pi$ gives 50.
optionRationale.2: $100\pi$ is the angular frequency in rad/s, not the frequency in Hz.
optionRationale.3: 314 is the value of $100\pi$, again the angular frequency rather than the frequency.

questions.objective: Read angular frequency and frequency from the equation of an alternating current

questions.stem: The domestic AC supply in India is rated 220 V. The peak value of this voltage is approximately
questions.explanation: Voltages quoted for the mains are rms values. For a sinusoidal voltage the peak value is $\sqrt{2}$ times the rms value, so the peak is $V_0 = 1.414 \times 220 \approx 311\,\text{V}$. Insulation in household wiring must be able to withstand this peak voltage.

optionRationale.1: This divides 220 by $\sqrt{2}$, treating 220 V as the peak value.
optionRationale.2: 220 V is the rms value, not the peak value.
optionRationale.4: This doubles the rms value; doubling the peak would give the peak-to-peak value, about 622 V.

questions.objective: Convert between rms and peak values of an alternating voltage

questions.stem: The current in a circuit is $i = 4\sin\omega t + 3\cos\omega t$ (in amperes). The rms value of this current is
questions.explanation: The two terms are sinusoids of the same frequency that are $90^\circ$ out of phase, so their phasors are perpendicular. The resultant is a single sinusoid of amplitude $I_0 = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5\,\text{A}$. Its rms value is therefore $I_0/\sqrt{2} = 5/1.414 = 3.54\,\text{A}$.

optionRationale.2: This adds the amplitudes arithmetically (7 A) before dividing by $\sqrt{2}$; perpendicular phasors must be added by Pythagoras.
optionRationale.3: 5.0 A is the peak value of the resultant current, not its rms value.
optionRationale.4: This divides the peak by 2 instead of by $\sqrt{2}$.

questions.objective: Combine two sinusoidal currents in quadrature and find the rms value

questions.stem: A sinusoidal alternating current has a peak value of 10 A. Its average value over a positive half cycle is
questions.explanation: Averaging $I_0\sin\omega t$ over a half cycle gives $\frac{1}{T/2}\int_0^{T/2}I_0\sin\omega t\,dt = 2I_0/\pi$. With a peak of 10 A this is $20/\pi = 6.37\,\text{A}$. Over a complete cycle the average would be zero, because the positive and negative halves cancel.

optionRationale.1: Zero is the average over a full cycle, not over a half cycle.
optionRationale.2: 7.07 A is the rms value, $I_0/\sqrt{2}$, which is larger than the half-cycle average.
optionRationale.4: 10 A is the peak value; the current is below the peak for most of the half cycle.

questions.objective: Distinguish half-cycle average, rms and peak values of AC

questions.stem: A 50 Hz alternating current starts from zero at $t = 0$. The minimum time after which its instantaneous value becomes equal to its rms value is
questions.explanation: Write the current as $i = I_0\sin\omega t$ and set it equal to the rms value $I_0/\sqrt{2}$. This gives $\sin\omega t = 1/\sqrt{2}$, which is first satisfied when the phase equals $\pi/4$, that is one eighth of a complete cycle. The period of a 50 Hz current is 20 ms, so the required time is one eighth of 20 ms, which is 2.5 ms.

optionRationale.2: 5 ms is $T/4$, the time to reach the peak value, not the rms value.
optionRationale.3: 1.25 ms is $T/16$; the phase needed is $\pi/4$, which is one eighth of $2\pi$.
optionRationale.4: 10 ms is half a period, when the current is back at zero.

questions.objective: Relate the phase of a sinusoid to time and to the rms value

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The heating effect of an alternating current is described by its rms value rather than by its average value.
Reason (R): The average of a sinusoidal current over a complete cycle is zero, whereas the heat produced in a resistor depends on the square of the current.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The heat produced in a resistor is proportional to $i^2$, which is never negative, so an alternating current certainly heats a resistor. Its full-cycle average, however, is zero and says nothing about heating. The rms value, the square root of the mean of $i^2$, is exactly the quantity that measures heating. So R correctly explains A.

optionRationale.2: R gives precisely the reason why the average is useless and the mean of $i^2$ is needed.
optionRationale.3: R is true: the full-cycle average is zero and heating goes as $i^2$.
optionRationale.4: A is true: rms values are defined by the heating effect.

questions.objective: Explain why rms values are used for alternating currents

questions.stem: The inductive reactance of a pure inductor of 0.5 H connected to a 50 Hz supply is approximately
questions.explanation: The inductive reactance is the product of the angular frequency and the inductance, $X_L = 2\pi\nu L$. Substituting a frequency of 50 Hz and an inductance of 0.5 H gives $X_L = 2 \times 3.14 \times 50 \times 0.5 = 157\,\Omega$. This value would double if the supply frequency were doubled, because the reactance of an inductor is directly proportional to frequency.

optionRationale.1: This is $\nu L$; the factor $2\pi$ has been left out.
optionRationale.2: This uses $\pi\nu L$ instead of $2\pi\nu L$.
optionRationale.4: This uses $4\pi\nu L$, double the correct value, or takes $\omega = 2\pi\nu$ twice.

questions.objective: Calculate inductive reactance

questions.stem: A $10\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. The rms current in the circuit is approximately
questions.explanation: First find the opposition offered by the capacitor, its capacitive reactance: $X_C = 1/(2\pi\nu C) = 1/(2\pi \times 50 \times 10\times10^{-6}) = 318\,\Omega$. The rms current is then the rms voltage divided by this reactance, $I = 220/318 = 0.69\,\text{A}$. Because the circuit is purely capacitive, this current leads the voltage by a quarter of a cycle.

optionRationale.1: This halves the correct current, as if the frequency or capacitance were halved.
optionRationale.3: This doubles the correct current; it is the value for a 100 Hz supply.
optionRationale.4: This divides the reactance by 100 rather than dividing the voltage by the reactance.

questions.objective: Calculate capacitive reactance and current in a purely capacitive circuit

questions.stem: The frequency of the AC source connected to a coil and, separately, to a capacitor is doubled. The inductive reactance $X_L$ of the coil and the capacitive reactance $X_C$ of the capacitor change as follows:
options: inductive reactance doubles and capacitive reactance doubles
inductive reactance halves and capacitive reactance doubles
inductive reactance doubles and capacitive reactance halves
questions.explanation: Inductive reactance $X_L = 2\pi\nu L$ is directly proportional to frequency, so it doubles. Capacitive reactance $X_C = 1/(2\pi\nu C)$ is inversely proportional to frequency, so it halves. An inductor opposes high frequencies more, while a capacitor opposes them less.

optionRationale.1: $X_C$ is inversely proportional to frequency, so it cannot double.
optionRationale.2: The dependences are reversed: $X_L$ increases and $X_C$ decreases with frequency.
optionRationale.4: Both reactances depend on frequency; only a resistance is independent of it.

questions.objective: Describe how reactances vary with frequency

questions.stem: Match each AC circuit in List-I with the phase relation between its current and the source voltage in List-II.

right: Current lags voltage by an angle between 0 and $\pi/2$
Current and voltage are in phase

questions.explanation: In a resistor current and voltage are in phase (A-III). In a pure inductor the current lags by $\pi/2$ (B-IV). In a pure capacitor the current leads by $\pi/2$ (C-I). A series LCR circuit with $X_L > X_C$ is inductive with $\tan\phi = (X_L - X_C)/R$ finite, so the current lags by an angle between 0 and $\pi/2$ (D-II).

optionRationale.1: The inductor and capacitor are swapped: the capacitor's current leads, the inductor's lags.
optionRationale.3: A resistor has zero phase difference, and the LCR circuit with resistance cannot have exactly zero phase difference unless $X_L = X_C$.
optionRationale.4: A pure inductor has exactly $\pi/2$ lag, while the LCR circuit has a smaller lag because of R.

questions.objective: Identify the phase relations in R, L, C and LCR circuits

questions.stem: A capacitor allows alternating current to flow in a circuit but blocks a steady direct current. This is because
options: the capacitive reactance becomes infinite when the frequency is zero
the capacitive reactance is zero for direct current
charge passes through the dielectric only when the voltage alternates
a capacitor has very high resistance only for alternating current
questions.explanation: The capacitive reactance is $X_C = 1/(2\pi\nu C)$. For a steady direct current the frequency is zero, so $X_C$ becomes infinitely large and no steady current can flow once the capacitor is charged. With AC the capacitor charges and discharges continually, so current flows in the connecting wires.

optionRationale.2: This is the reverse: $X_C$ is infinite, not zero, at zero frequency.
optionRationale.3: No charge crosses the dielectric in either case; AC flows because of repeated charging and discharging.
optionRationale.4: A capacitor offers less, not more, opposition to AC than to DC.

questions.objective: Explain why a capacitor blocks DC using capacitive reactance

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the variation of opposition to current with the frequency $\nu$ of the source:
A. A graph of $X_L$ against $\nu$ is a straight line passing through the origin.
B. A graph of $X_C$ against $\nu$ is a rectangular hyperbola.
C. The resistance of an ideal resistor increases linearly with $\nu$.
D. At very high frequencies an ideal capacitor behaves almost like a short circuit.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.explanation:
Since $X_L = 2\pi
u L$ is proportional to frequency, its graph is a straight line through the origin (A true). Since $X_C = 1/(2\pi
u C)$, the product $X_C
u$ is constant, a rectangular hyperbola (B true). Resistance does not depend on frequency (C false). As frequency becomes very large, $X_C$ tends to zero, so the capacitor acts like a short circuit (D true).

optionRationale.1: D is also correct, because $X_C$ approaches zero at very high frequency.
optionRationale.3: C is false: an ideal resistance is independent of frequency.
optionRationale.4: C is false, and B is true.

questions.objective: Interpret graphs of reactance and resistance against frequency

questions.stem: A series LCR circuit has $R = 40\,\Omega$, $X_L = 50\,\Omega$ and $X_C = 20\,\Omega$. It is connected to a 200 V (rms) AC source. The rms current in the circuit is
questions.explanation: The impedance of a series LCR circuit combines the resistance with the net reactance: $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = \sqrt{40^2 + 30^2} = 50\,\Omega$. The rms current is the rms voltage divided by the impedance, $I = 200/50 = 4\,\text{A}$. Since the inductive reactance is larger than the capacitive reactance, the circuit is inductive and the current lags the voltage.

optionRationale.1: This divides by R alone; that would be correct only at resonance.
optionRationale.2: This takes the impedance as $100\,\Omega$, for example by adding R and the net reactance without squaring.
optionRationale.3: This adds R, $X_L$ and $X_C$ arithmetically (110 Ω); reactances subtract and combine with R by Pythagoras.

questions.objective: Calculate the impedance and current of a series LCR circuit

questions.stem: In a series LCR circuit connected to an AC source, the rms voltages measured across the resistor, the inductor and the capacitor are 120 V, 250 V and 90 V respectively. The rms voltage of the source is
questions.explanation: The voltages across L and C are opposite in phase, so their net value is $250 - 90 = 160\,\text{V}$, which is at $90^\circ$ to the resistor voltage. The source voltage is the phasor sum, $V = \sqrt{120^2 + 160^2} = \sqrt{40000} = 200\,\text{V}$. Note that the inductor voltage alone exceeds the source voltage.

optionRationale.1: This adds the three voltages arithmetically, ignoring their phase differences.
optionRationale.3: This adds $V_R$ and $V_L - V_C$ arithmetically; they are perpendicular phasors.
optionRationale.4: 160 V is only the net reactive voltage $V_L - V_C$; the resistor voltage must be included.

questions.objective: Add voltages in a series LCR circuit using a phasor diagram

questions.stem: A series LCR circuit has $R = 100\,\Omega$, $X_L = 300\,\Omega$ and $X_C = 200\,\Omega$. The phase difference between the current and the source voltage, and its sense, are
options: 45°, with the current lagging the voltage
45°, with the current leading the voltage
60°, with the current lagging the voltage
90°, with the current lagging the voltage
questions.explanation: The phase angle is found from $\tan\phi = (X_L - X_C)/R = (300 - 200)/100 = 1$, so the angle is $45^\circ$. Because the inductive reactance is larger than the capacitive reactance, the circuit behaves inductively, and in an inductive circuit the current lags behind the source voltage. The power factor of the circuit is therefore $\cos 45^\circ$, about 0.707.

optionRationale.2: The current leads only when $X_C$ is larger than $X_L$.
optionRationale.3: $\tan 60^\circ = 1.73$, but here $\tan\phi = 1$.
optionRationale.4: A $90^\circ$ lag needs a purely inductive circuit; the resistance makes the angle smaller.

questions.objective: Find the phase angle and decide whether a series LCR circuit is inductive or capacitive

questions.stem: A series circuit has $R = 120\,\Omega$, $L = 0.1\,\text{H}$ and $C = 20\,\mu\text{F}$, and is connected to a 260 V (rms) source of angular frequency $1000\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$. The average power consumed by the circuit is
questions.explanation: First find the reactances: $X_L = \omega L = 100\,\Omega$ and $X_C = 1/(\omega C) = 50\,\Omega$. The impedance is then $Z = \sqrt{120^2 + 50^2} = 130\,\Omega$ and the rms current is $260/130 = 2\,\text{A}$. Average power is consumed only in the resistance, so $P = I^2R = 4 \times 120 = 480\,\text{W}$. The same answer follows from the apparent power multiplied by the power factor, 120/130.

optionRationale.1: 520 W is the apparent power $VI$; it must be multiplied by the power factor $12/13$.
optionRationale.2: This is $I^2$ times the net reactance; reactances consume no average power.
optionRationale.4: This doubles the correct power, for example by using peak instead of rms values without the factor one half.

questions.objective: Calculate the average power in a series LCR circuit

questions.stem: Refer to the phasor diagram (b) drawn for the series LCR circuit shown. Which statement about the circuit is correct?
options: The circuit is capacitive and the current leads the source voltage
The circuit is inductive and the source voltage leads the current by φ, where $\tan\phi = (V_L - V_C)/V_R$
The source voltage is equal to $V_R + V_L + V_C$
The circuit is at resonance because $V_R$ lies along the current
questions.explanation: In the diagram the inductor voltage phasor is longer than the capacitor voltage phasor, so the net reactive voltage points upward and the resultant source voltage lies above the current phasor. The voltage therefore leads the current by the angle $\phi$, with $\tan\phi = (V_L - V_C)/V_R$, and the circuit is inductive.

optionRationale.1: The current would lead only if $V_C$ were larger than $V_L$; in the figure $V_L$ is larger.
optionRationale.3: The three voltages are not in phase; they add as phasors, not arithmetically.
optionRationale.4: $V_R$ always lies along the current; resonance needs $V_L = V_C$, which is not the case here.

questions.objective: Interpret a phasor diagram of a series LCR circuit

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about phasors used to represent alternating quantities:
A. A phasor rotates anticlockwise about the origin with angular speed $\omega$.
B. The length of a phasor represents the peak value of the quantity.
C. The instantaneous value of the quantity is the projection of its phasor on the vertical axis.
D. For a pure capacitor, the voltage and current phasors are parallel.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.explanation: By convention a phasor has a length equal to the peak value, rotates anticlockwise at $\omega$, and its vertical projection gives the instantaneous value, so A, B and C are correct. For a pure capacitor the current leads the voltage by $90^\circ$, so the two phasors are perpendicular, not parallel; D is false.

optionRationale.2: B and C are also correct, and D is false.
optionRationale.3: D is false: the phasors for a capacitor are at right angles.
optionRationale.4: D is false, so not all four statements are correct.

questions.objective: State the conventions used in phasor diagrams

questions.stem: A series LCR circuit has $L = 0.1\,\text{H}$ and $C = 10\,\mu\text{F}$. Its resonant frequency is approximately
questions.explanation: The resonant angular frequency depends only on the inductance and the capacitance: $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC} = 1/\sqrt{0.1 \times 10^{-5}} = 1/\sqrt{10^{-6}} = 1000\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$. To express it in hertz, divide by $2\pi$: $\nu_0 = 1000/6.28 \approx 159\,\text{Hz}$. The resistance of the circuit does not change this value; it only affects how sharp the resonance is.

optionRationale.1: 1000 is the resonant angular frequency in rad/s; divide by $2\pi$ to get hertz.
optionRationale.2: This divides by $\pi$ instead of $2\pi$.
optionRationale.3: 50 Hz is the mains frequency, unrelated to the given L and C.

questions.objective: Calculate the resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true for a series LCR circuit at resonance?
options: The impedance is minimum and equal to R
questions.explanation: At resonance $X_L = X_C$, so the net reactance cancels and the impedance falls to its minimum value, $Z = R$. As a result the current is maximum and in phase with the voltage, giving a power factor of 1. The statement that the impedance is maximum is therefore false.

optionRationale.1: This is true: the reactances cancel, leaving only R.
optionRationale.2: This is true: minimum impedance gives maximum current.
optionRationale.3: This is true: current and voltage are in phase, so $\cos\phi = 1$.

questions.objective: State the properties of a series LCR circuit at resonance

questions.stem: A coil of inductance 25 mH is to be used with a capacitor so that the series circuit resonates at a frequency of 1.0 kHz. The required capacitance is approximately
questions.explanation:
Rearranging the resonance condition $
u_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ gives $C = 1/(4\pi^2
u_0^2L)$. Substituting $4\pi^2 \approx 39.5$, $
u_0^2 = 10^6\,	ext{Hz}^2$ and $L = 0.025\,	ext{H}$ gives $C = 1/(39.5 	imes 10^6 	imes 0.025) = 1.01	imes10^{-6}\,	ext{F}$, which is about one microfarad. This is how a receiver is tuned: the capacitance is chosen to bring the resonance to the wanted frequency.

optionRationale.1: This is ten times too small; check the power of ten from $\nu_0^2 = 10^6$.
optionRationale.3: This is ten times too large.
optionRationale.4: This omits a factor of 4 or squares $2\pi$ incorrectly.

questions.objective: Choose a capacitance for resonance at a given frequency, as in radio tuning

questions.stem: A series LCR circuit with $R = 10\,\Omega$ is connected to a 20 V (rms) source at its resonant frequency, at which $X_L = X_C = 100\,\Omega$. The rms voltage across the inductor is
questions.explanation: At resonance the impedance is just R, so the current is $I = 20/10 = 2\,\text{A}$. The voltage across the inductor is $IX_L = 2 \times 100 = 200\,\text{V}$, ten times the source voltage; this ratio is the quality factor $Q = X_L/R = 10$. The capacitor has an equal and opposite 200 V across it.

optionRationale.1: This assumes no voltage magnification; at resonance $V_L = QV$, which can greatly exceed the source voltage.
optionRationale.2: This uses a current of 1 A; at resonance the current is $V/R = 2\,\text{A}$.
optionRationale.4: This divides instead of multiplying by the quality factor.

questions.objective: Calculate voltage magnification at resonance

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A series LCR circuit at resonance behaves as a purely resistive circuit.
Reason (R): At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal, so the impedance equals R and the current is in phase with the applied voltage.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: At resonance $X_L = X_C$, so the net reactance is zero and $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + 0} = R$. The phase angle given by $\tan\phi = 0$ is zero, so voltage and current are in phase, exactly as in a resistor. R states the cause of the behaviour described in A, so it is the correct explanation.

optionRationale.2: R is not an unrelated fact; equal reactances are exactly why the circuit acts resistively.
optionRationale.3: R is true: at resonance $X_L = X_C$ and $Z = R$.
optionRationale.4: A is true: the circuit draws current in phase with the voltage and $Z = R$.

questions.objective: Explain why a resonant series LCR circuit is purely resistive

questions.stem: A series LCR circuit has $L = 0.5\,\text{H}$, $C = 5\,\mu\text{F}$ and $R = 10\,\Omega$. The quality factor of the circuit is approximately
questions.explanation: For a series LCR circuit the quality factor can be written $Q = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{L/C}$. Here the ratio of inductance to capacitance is $0.5/(5\times10^{-6}) = 10^5$, and its square root is about 316. Dividing by the resistance of 10 ohms gives a quality factor of about 31.6. As a check, the resonant angular frequency is about 632 rad/s, and multiplying by L and dividing by R gives the same value.

optionRationale.1: 10 is the resistance in ohms, not the quality factor.
optionRationale.2: This divides by 100 instead of 10; recheck $\sqrt{10^5} \approx 316$.
optionRationale.3: 316 is $\sqrt{L/C}$ before dividing by R.

questions.objective: Calculate the quality factor of a series resonant circuit

questions.stem: The power factor of a circuit containing only an ideal inductor connected to an AC source is
questions.explanation: In an ideal inductor the current lags the voltage by exactly $90^\circ$. The power factor is $\cos\phi = \cos 90^\circ = 0$, so the average power is zero: energy stored in the magnetic field during one quarter cycle is returned to the source in the next.

optionRationale.2: A power factor of 1 belongs to a purely resistive circuit or to an LCR circuit at resonance.
optionRationale.3: 0.5 corresponds to a phase angle of $60^\circ$, not $90^\circ$.
optionRationale.4: 0.707 corresponds to a phase angle of $45^\circ$, as when R equals the net reactance.

questions.objective: Recall the power factor of a purely inductive circuit

questions.stem: In an AC circuit the rms voltage is 220 V, the rms current is 5 A and the current lags the voltage by $60^\circ$. The average power consumed is
questions.explanation: The average power is $P = VI\cos\phi$. Here $VI = 220 \times 5 = 1100\,\text{VA}$ is the apparent power and $\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$ is the power factor, so $P = 1100 \times 0.5 = 550\,\text{W}$. The rest of the apparent power is associated with the wattless component of the current.

optionRationale.1: 1100 W is the apparent power; it ignores the power factor.
optionRationale.2: This uses $\cos 30^\circ$ instead of $\cos 60^\circ$.
optionRationale.4: The power is zero only when the phase difference is exactly $90^\circ$.

questions.objective: Use P = VI cos φ

questions.stem: The voltage and current in an AC circuit are $v = 100\sin(100t)$ V and $i = 2\sin(100t - \pi/3)$ A. The average power dissipated in the circuit is
questions.explanation: Reading the two expressions, the peak voltage is 100 V, the peak current is 2 A, and the current lags the voltage by $\pi/3$, that is $60^\circ$. With peak values the average power is $P = \tfrac{1}{2}V_0I_0\cos\phi = 0.5 \times 100 \times 2 \times 0.5 = 50\,\text{W}$. The same answer follows from rms values, because the product of the rms voltage and rms current is 100 and the power factor is one half.

optionRationale.1: This omits either the factor one half or the power factor.
optionRationale.3: This uses $\cos 30^\circ$; the phase difference is $\pi/3 = 60^\circ$.
optionRationale.4: This multiplies the peak values directly and ignores both the factor one half and the power factor.

questions.objective: Calculate average power from instantaneous expressions of voltage and current

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Electricity supply companies discourage industrial consumers from operating at a low power factor.
Reason (R): For the same power delivered at a given voltage, a lower power factor requires a larger current, which increases the $I^2R$ losses in the supply lines.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Since $P = VI\cos\phi$, the current needed for a given power is $I = P/(V\cos\phi)$, which grows as the power factor falls. The larger current wastes more energy as $I^2R$ heat in cables and transformers, without delivering more useful power. This is exactly why supply companies penalise low power factors, so R explains A.

optionRationale.2: R is the actual reason for the policy described in A.
optionRationale.3: R is true: current is inversely proportional to the power factor for fixed P and V.
optionRationale.4: A is true: low power factor is discouraged and often penalised.

questions.objective: Explain the practical importance of power factor

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The average power consumed by an ideal capacitor connected to an AC source is zero.
Reason (R): No current flows in a circuit containing a capacitor connected to an AC source.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: A is true: the current leads the voltage by $90^\circ$, the power factor is zero, and the energy stored in the capacitor during one quarter cycle is returned during the next. R is false: an alternating current does flow in the circuit, of rms value $V/X_C$, because the capacitor is continually charged and discharged.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot be the explanation.
optionRationale.2: R is false: a capacitor passes alternating current.
optionRationale.4: A is true: the average power in an ideal capacitor is zero.

questions.objective: Distinguish zero average power from zero current in a capacitive circuit

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): In a series LCR circuit, the rms voltage of the source equals the sum of the rms voltages across R, L and C.
Reason (R): The voltages across R, L and C are not in phase with one another, so they must be added as phasors.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The voltage across R is in phase with the current, the voltage across L leads by $90^\circ$ and the voltage across C lags by $90^\circ$. They must therefore be added as phasors, $V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$, which is less than their arithmetic sum. So R is true and A is false.

optionRationale.1: A is false, so this combination cannot be correct.
optionRationale.2: A is false; the arithmetic sum exceeds the source voltage.
optionRationale.3: A is the false statement and R is the true one.

questions.objective: Recognise that voltages in a series LCR circuit add as phasors

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The reactance of an inductor is larger for an alternating current of higher frequency.
Reason (R): An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field when a current flows through it.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: A is true: $X_L = 2\pi\nu L$ grows with frequency, because a faster-changing current produces a larger back emf. R is also true, since the stored energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}LI^2$. However, energy storage does not explain the frequency dependence; that comes from the back emf being proportional to the rate of change of current. So R is not the explanation of A.

optionRationale.1: Energy storage does not explain why the opposition increases with frequency; the rate of change of current does.
optionRationale.3: R is true: an inductor stores $\tfrac{1}{2}LI^2$ in its magnetic field.
optionRationale.4: A is true: $X_L$ is proportional to frequency.

questions.objective: Identify the cause of the frequency dependence of inductive reactance

questions.stem: In an AC circuit the rms current is 10 A and it lags the voltage by $30^\circ$. The wattless component of the current is
questions.explanation: The current can be resolved into a component along the voltage and a component perpendicular to it. The perpendicular part is the wattless component, $I\sin\phi = 10 \times \sin 30^\circ = 10 \times 0.5 = 5\,\text{A}$. The component along the voltage, $I\cos\phi = 8.66\,\text{A}$, is the active part that actually delivers power to the circuit.

optionRationale.2: 8.66 A is the active (wattful) component $I\cos\phi$.
optionRationale.3: 10 A is the whole current; only part of it is wattless.
optionRationale.4: The wattless current is zero only when the current is in phase with the voltage.

questions.objective: Calculate the wattless component of an alternating current

questions.stem: A circuit connected to a 200 V (rms) supply draws an rms current of 5 A and consumes an average power of 600 W. The wattless component of the current is
questions.explanation: First find the power factor from the given data: $\cos\phi = P/(VI) = 600/(200 \times 5) = 0.6$. It follows that $\sin\phi = \sqrt{1 - 0.36} = 0.8$. The wattless component of the current is therefore $I\sin\phi = 5 \times 0.8 = 4\,\text{A}$, while the active component, which carries all of the power, is $5 \times 0.6 = 3\,\text{A}$.

optionRationale.1: 3 A is the active component $I\cos\phi$, the one that carries power.
optionRationale.2: 5 A is the total current, not its wattless component.
optionRationale.3: 0.6 is the power factor, a pure number, not a current.

questions.objective: Find the wattless current from voltage, current and power

questions.stem: A choke coil is preferred to a resistor for reducing the current in an AC circuit (for example, in an old tube-light fitting) because
options: the choke wastes very little power, since its current is nearly wattless
the choke increases the frequency of the supply
the choke has a higher resistance than any resistor
the choke makes the power factor of the circuit equal to 1
questions.explanation: A choke is an inductor with very small resistance. It limits the current through its inductive reactance, and the current through a nearly pure inductor is almost $90^\circ$ out of phase with the voltage across it, so it is nearly wattless and very little energy is dissipated. A resistor doing the same job would waste $I^2R$ as heat.

optionRationale.2: No passive component changes the frequency of the supply.
optionRationale.3: A choke has very low resistance; it limits current through reactance, not resistance.
optionRationale.4: Adding an inductor lowers the power factor; it does not make it 1.

questions.objective: Explain the use of a choke coil in terms of wattless current

questions.stem: In the phasor diagram shown, the current I lags the voltage V by an angle φ. Which component of the current is responsible for the average power consumed in the circuit?
options: I sin φ, perpendicular to V
neither component, because the average power in an AC circuit is always zero
questions.explanation: Only the part of the current that is in phase with the voltage delivers net energy. In the figure this is the component along V, $I\cos\phi$, so the average power is $P = V(I\cos\phi)$. The perpendicular component $I\sin\phi$ is wattless and gives zero average power.

optionRationale.1: $I\sin\phi$ is $90^\circ$ out of phase with V; it is the wattless component.
optionRationale.3: Using the full current gives the apparent power $VI$, not the true power.
optionRationale.4: The average power is zero only for purely reactive circuits; here $\cos\phi$ is not zero.

questions.objective: Identify the active and wattless components of current on a phasor diagram

questions.stem: The figure shows resonance curves for two series LCR circuits with the same L and C but resistances $R_1 < R_2$. Which circuit has the larger bandwidth, and why?
options: The circuit with R₁, because its peak current is larger
The circuit with R₂, because the bandwidth equals R/L
Both have the same bandwidth, because L and C are the same
The circuit with R₁, because its quality factor is larger
questions.explanation: The bandwidth between the half-power frequencies of a series LCR circuit is $2\Delta\omega = R/L$. With the same inductance, the circuit with the larger resistance, $R_2$, has the larger bandwidth and the broader, lower curve. Its quality factor $\omega_0L/R$ is correspondingly smaller.

optionRationale.1: A taller peak goes with a narrower, not wider, resonance.
optionRationale.3: The bandwidth depends on R as well as L, so the two circuits differ.
optionRationale.4: A larger quality factor means a smaller bandwidth, since $2\Delta\omega = \omega_0/Q$.

questions.objective: Relate bandwidth and sharpness of resonance to resistance

questions.stem: In a series LCR circuit connected to an AC source, the phase difference between the voltage across the inductor and the voltage across the capacitor is
questions.explanation: The same current flows through both. The voltage across the inductor leads this current by $90^\circ$ and the voltage across the capacitor lags it by $90^\circ$. The two voltages are therefore $180^\circ$ out of phase, which is why they partly cancel and why the reactances subtract in the impedance formula.

optionRationale.1: They would be in phase only if both led or both lagged the current by the same angle.
optionRationale.2: $90^\circ$ is the phase difference between each of them and the resistor voltage, not between each other.
optionRationale.4: There is no $45^\circ$ relation between ideal L and C voltages.

questions.objective: Determine the phase relation between inductor and capacitor voltages in series
